of difficulties, to dispel
the concern of
being a harmful and damaging plant to
health, supporting this
idea men of the greatest instruction, who dissuaded
people
from eating this root, fearful
of some bad quality of it, considering that it is of
the natural family
of the Solanums, which for the most
part
are poisonous.
For the same reason today
foreigners discard from their gardens
the eggplant, and even do not cultivate the tomato in the most gar
dens. We should lament the almost general neglect,
and the little care that has been noted until
these last
times in promoting the cultivation of this plant; and
it is to be desired, that it be introduced generally through
the entire kingdom, and that good patricians make known
the utilities that may
result from
extending its
cultivation so that each one may seek its greater increase.
It should be noted in this place, that what contributed
more
than anything else to the spread at the
beginning of the introduction of this plant were some ideas
not
favorable and to the discredit of the potatoes, it was
that through ignorance, carelessness and lack of suffi
cient cultivation, they take, when not earthed as they
should, and with
their roots exposed to
the
impression of the sharp suns and the air, a dark
green color, and an acrid taste, of bad flavor, and of ba
d quality. With proper cultivation they grow
sweet, of good flavor and healthy, and thus are unfounded
and baseless
the bad properties that have been
wanted to be attributed to
this useful production. The experience of
Ireland, Scotland, England and other peoples who
feed on potatoes,
demonstrates to us the falsity of
such concerns, and clearly shows us its
healthy and excellent qualities.
Thus we
see that the
Irish, who for three parts of the year
maintain themselves for three of
this root, far from suffering any
harm to their health, the young men grow the most
robust and
strong of
almost all
Europe.
Sowing. The cultivators were not ignorant
that the potato could be propagated by the pods of the
tomatillos in which it converts by the fertilization of
the flower; but this method has not been generally practiced,
as it is slower, and takes two or three years for
the potatoes to form well.
Some more curious and
eager to
obtain
new varieties, have executed it, fully achieving their intent. The method for
this sowing is to mark some beds or mounds of
loose soil and well-worked crumb, de-clodded and
enriched with compost. Scattering by the month of
March very thinly the seed in furrows, distant from
eight to
twelve fingers, on
their surface, it will sprout in
the spring
of the same year, and will be earthed as they
grow, working the intervals
between
the furrows, weeding all
bad grass, and thinning out the plants that have grown too thick; since
they must remain apart from each other
in the lines
of
eight to ten fingers. In this way they will have space and capacity
to spread and nourish, and can more easily
obtain excellent strains and of good
size.
From all these
plants of sowing, usable potatoes for
domestic use will not be obtained until
the second or
third year. At that time, all those
plants will be noted with care, more
lush, grown, and of greater growth, and the clumps that
have produced
the largest potatoes, and
different from those commonly cultivated by
color, flavor, shape,
precocity or other similar
circumstance more notable. Cultivated these new
varieties with the most
exquisite care, they will be
multiplied quickly, and new
species will be begun. The potatoes of
sowing will be harvested in the autumn
.

The Réaumur thermometer must be maintained from seven to ten degrees above zero so that the tomato plants may grow with vigor. The water for watering will be tempered before using it, for if it were too cold, it might harm rather than benefit. Every damaged, dry, or rotten leaf will be removed with care, and if any plant should rot, it will be separated from the proximity of the others so as not to spread the disease.

Harvest. The tomatoes are gathered from the plants as soon as they have turned red, for although on many occasions they are collected green with the intention of keeping them for several days, they always retain a certain unpleasant roughness that should be avoided.

Harvest for seed. The tomatoes for seed will be chosen among the roundest, purest, smoothest fruits, and with firm flesh. The seed will not be separated from the flesh, unless this begins to rot. In this state, the tomatoes will be crushed in a garden bell with water, dissolving the pulp well with the hands, and then the water will be poured off gently, and the pipings dried to keep them. They remain good for two or three years, fit to germinate.

Economic and medicinal uses. The tomatoes are eaten raw with salt; but it is a very cold food, and not one of the most wholesome: they are also eaten cooked in various ways. Their daily use is for sauces and preserves, communicating a very agreeable acid taste. Some pickle them in vinegar with salt and black pepper, making some incisions so that they may be penetrated more thoroughly by the vinegar. In this condition, they are kept for a long time without rotting; but for this purpose, tomatoes not very ripe should be chosen. The fruit of the tomato excites the appetite, and strengthens the stomach weakened by excessive heat.
